claims.claim: Reconciliation runs on a 20-hour Senate debate clock rather than a different vote threshold
claims.sourceSpan: Debate in the Senate on any reconciliation bill reported under subsection (b), and all amendments thereto and debatable motions and appeals in connection therewith, shall be limited to not more than 20 hours.

claims.claim: Because debate is limited, cloture is not necessary to reach a final vote
claims.sourceSpan: A distinctive feature of reconciliation is that debate time in the Senate is limited, which means cloture (and its requisite three-fifths majority vote) is not necessary to reach a vote on final passage.

claims.claim: The Byrd rule bars extraneous matter from a reconciliation bill
claims.sourceSpan: The Byrd rule establishes six tests used to identify extraneous matter.

claims.claim: Directives cover spending, revenue and the debt limit
claims.sourceSpan: There are three types of reconciliation directives: to change laws providing for spending, to change laws providing for revenues, and to change the public debt limit.

claims.claim: Reconciliation is an expedited process made available under Section 310 of the Congressional Budget Act of 1974
claims.sourceSpan: an expedited process made available under Section 310 of the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 (the Budget Act)

claims.claim: The distinctive feature is a Senate debate limit, so cloture is not necessary to reach final passage
claims.sourceSpan: A distinctive feature of reconciliation is that debate time in the Senate is limited, which means cloture (and its requisite three-fifths majority vote) is not necessary to reach a vote on final passage.

claims.claim: Passage takes a majority of Senators present and voting
claims.sourceSpan: The votes of only a majority of Senators present and voting are needed to pass a bill on the floor.
claims.section: Filibusters and Cloture in the Senate, body text on passage thresholds

claims.claim: The Vice President votes only when the Senate is equally divided
claims.sourceSpan: The Vice President of the United States shall be President of the Senate, but shall have no Vote, unless they be equally divided.

claims.claim: Reconciliation has been used for entitlement reform, new entitlements, deficit balancing and tax reform in named years
claims.sourceSpan: It has been used to reform entitlement programs (1996 and 2025), create new ones (2010), balance the federal budget (1997), and enact broad-based tax reform (2001, 2003, 2017, and 2025).

claims.claim: Reconciliation directives are a necessary step to use the expedited procedures
claims.sourceSpan: Reconciliation directives (also known as reconciliation instructions ) are a necessary step if Congress seeks to exercise the expedited procedures enumerated in the Budget Act.

claims.claim: There are three types of directive: spending, revenue and the public debt limit
claims.sourceSpan: There are three types of reconciliation directives: to change laws providing for spending, to change laws providing for revenues, and to change the public debt limit.

claims.claim: A fourth instruction, to change the deficit, is treated as a combination of revenue and spending instructions
claims.sourceSpan: A fourth instruction—to change the deficit—is interpreted as a combination of both revenue and spending instructions.

claims.claim: Instructed committees submit recommendations to the Budget Committee, which reports them without substantive revision
claims.sourceSpan: shall promptly make such determination and recommendations and submit such recommendations to the Committee on the Budget of its House, which, upon receiving all such recommendations, shall report to its House reconciliation legislation carrying out all such recommendations without any substantive revision.

claims.claim: The Senate debate limit on a reconciliation bill is not more than 20 hours, covering amendments, debatable motions and appeals
claims.sourceSpan: Debate in the Senate on any reconciliation bill reported under subsection (b), and all amendments thereto and debatable motions and appeals in connection therewith, shall be limited to not more than 20 hours.

claims.claim: 641(e) is headed Procedure in Senate, so the 20-hour limit is a Senate limit and carries no House or conference figure
claims.sourceSpan: (e) Procedure in Senate

claims.claim: Inside the 20 hours, first-degree amendments get two hours and second-degree amendments, motions and appeals one hour
claims.sourceSpan: Debate time on any first-degree amendment is limited to no more than two hours equally divided between the mover and the manager of the reconciliation bill. Debate on any second-degree amendment, debatable motion, or appeal is limited to one hour.

claims.claim: Quorum-call time during an amendment counts against the limit, and all floor discussion counts toward the 20 hours, while time conducting votes does not
claims.sourceSpan: Time spent in a quorum call during consideration of an amendment counts against this limit. All time spent in discussion on the floor during this period (on the reconciliation bill or on any amendment, motion, or appeal) counts toward the 20-hour debate limit. Time spent conducting votes does not.

claims.claim: The Senate limit on a conference report is 10 hours, equally divided, with one hour on any motion or appeal
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, Section 305(c) limits debate on a conference report to 10 hours, equally divided, and debate on any motion or appeal is limited to one hour.

claims.claim: House consideration is structured by a special rule from the Rules Committee
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, consideration is typically structured by a special rule reported from the House Rules Committee, which sets the terms for debate and may permit specified amendments to be offered from the floor.

claims.claim: Amendments to reconciliation legislation must be germane
claims.sourceSpan: Amendments to reconciliation legislation must be germane

claims.claim: Section 310(e) prohibits Senate consideration of non-germane amendments
claims.sourceSpan: Section 310(e) of the Budget Act prohibits consideration in the Senate of non-germane amendments to reconciliation legislation, thereby limiting the ability of Senators to expand the scope of changes recommended by committees through amendments offered on the Senate floor.

claims.claim: Section 305 limits debate but not consideration
claims.sourceSpan: specifies a limit on debate but not consideration

claims.claim: After debate time expires Senators may still offer and decide amendments but not debate them
claims.sourceSpan: even after debate time has expired, Senators may continue to offer and decide additional amendments, but they cannot debate them

claims.claim: A vote-arama is structured by unanimous consent agreements making tranches of amendments in order
claims.sourceSpan: During a vote-arama, the Senate typically uses unanimous consent agreements to make tranches of amendments in order and to set the parameters for their consideration

claims.claim: The typical parameter is two minutes evenly divided, then a vote
claims.sourceSpan: usually two minutes to identify and briefly summarize the amendment, evenly divided between sides, followed by a vote

claims.claim: The section's official heading is Extraneous matter in reconciliation legislation
claims.sourceSpan: Extraneous matter in reconciliation legislation

claims.claim: CRS names Section 313 the Byrd rule
claims.sourceSpan: Section 313, also known as the Byrd rule,

claims.claim: It is named after its principal sponsor, Senator Robert C. Byrd
claims.sourceSpan: In 1985 and 1986, the Senate adopted the Byrd rule (named after its principal sponsor, Senator Robert C. Byrd) on a temporary basis as a means of curbing these practices.

claims.claim: The Byrd rule establishes six tests for extraneous matter
claims.sourceSpan: The Byrd rule establishes six tests used to identify extraneous matter.

claims.claim: Test 1: no change in outlays or revenues, including via terms and conditions
claims.sourceSpan: It does not produce a change in outlays or revenues, including changes resulting from a change in the "terms and conditions" under which outlays are made or revenues are collected (e.g., a change in the definition of qualified beneficiaries or a change in the definition of a person or entity subject to a tax).

claims.claim: Test 2: increases outlays or decreases revenues while the committee is out of compliance
claims.sourceSpan: It produces an increase in outlays or a decrease in revenues when the instructed committee is not in compliance with its reconciliation directives.

claims.claim: Test 3: outside the jurisdiction of the submitting committee
claims.sourceSpan: It is outside of the jurisdiction of the committee that submitted the title or provision for inclusion in the reconciliation measure.

claims.claim: Test 4: budgetary change merely incidental to the non-budgetary components
claims.sourceSpan: It produces a change in outlays or revenues that is merely incidental to the non-budgetary components of the provision.

claims.claim: Test 5: increases the deficit beyond the years covered
claims.sourceSpan: It would increase the deficit in any fiscal year beyond the years covered by the reconciliation measure.

claims.claim: Test 6: amends Title II of the Social Security Act
claims.sourceSpan: It would amend Title II of the Social Security Act (the Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance program)

claims.claim: A sustained Byrd point of order strikes only the offending matter
claims.sourceSpan: A point of order made under the Byrd rule is surgical: If sustained, the offending matter is stricken from the text, but the rest of the measure remains before the Senate.

claims.claim: Waiving requires three-fifths of Senators duly chosen and sworn, 60 with no more than one vacancy
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, a motion to waive any of these points of order requires the affirmative vote of three-fifths of Senators, duly chosen and sworn (60 Members in a Senate with no more than one vacancy).

claims.claim: The Senate adopted the Byrd rule temporarily in 1985 and 1986
claims.sourceSpan: In 1985 and 1986, the Senate adopted the Byrd rule (named after its principal sponsor, Senator Robert C. Byrd) on a temporary basis as a means of curbing these practices.

claims.claim: It became Section 313 of the Budget Act and permanent in 1990
claims.sourceSpan: In 1990, the Byrd rule was incorporated into the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 as Section 313 and made permanent (2 U.S.C. 644).

claims.claim: The Parliamentarian advises the presiding officer on the Senate's rules including the Byrd rule
claims.sourceSpan: As the Senate's expert on the chamber's rules, precedents, and practices, the Senate Parliamentarian advises the presiding officer on the floor regarding the Senate's rules, including the Byrd rule.

claims.claim: Reconciliation legislation receives preemptive scrutiny by the Parliamentarian with Senate staff
claims.sourceSpan: In recent practice, reconciliation legislation to be considered in the Senate has received preemptive scrutiny by the Senate Parliamentarian in conjunction with Senate staff.

claims.claim: That tradition is called a Byrd bath or Byrd scrub
claims.sourceSpan: This tradition, known as a "Byrd bath" or "Byrd scrub," allows for the identification of legislative text that would violate the Byrd rule in advance of its consideration on the floor.

claims.claim: REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep, independently re-confirmed against the statute): "Debate is limited to 20 hours total (10 for each chamber in conference, or 20 for the Senate on a House-passed bill)." 2 U.S.C. 641(e)(2) sets a flat Senate limit of not more than 20 hours and says nothing about the House, about conference, or about a per-chamber split. The real 10-hour figure is the SENATE limit on a conference report under Section 305(c) of the Budget Act, which CRS R48444 states; both figures are now given with the right subject.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED, and the same class the senate-procedure batch fixed on senate-filibuster and cloture-60-vote: "a simple majority of 51 votes rather than the 60 votes normally needed", "a simple majority (51 votes, or 50 plus the Vice President) is all that is required", and the page title "The Senate's 51-Vote Path Explained". Reconciliation does not change the passage threshold at all - CRS R48444: the debate limit "means cloture (and its requisite three-fifths majority vote) is not necessary to reach a vote on final passage." Passage is by a majority of Senators present and voting (CRS RL30360), and the Vice President votes only on an equal division (Constitution, Article I, Section 3). Title, meta description, og:title, og:description and JSON-LD headline all changed.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep + the House-procedure batch flag): "The Byrd Rule categorically bars reconciliation from touching Social Security, the OASDI trust funds, or the Social Security Act - a protection written into the 1985 Gramm-Rudman-Hollings Act." Three errors in one sentence. (1) The standalone bar is 2 U.S.C. 641(g), a separate point of order that applies in BOTH chambers and sends the bill back to committee; the Byrd rule reaches it only by cross-reference at 644(b)(1)(F), Senate-only, striking the provision. (2) The scope is title II of the Social Security Act, not the whole Act or the trust funds. (3) The Byrd rule itself dates to 1985-86 as a temporary Senate rule and became Section 313 in 1990. The page now separates the two protections and gives each its own statutory text.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED and contradicted (sweep S-RISK; also flagged by the House-procedure batch as a live contradiction with the freshly audited how-a-bill-becomes-law): "the traditional interpretation is that only one reconciliation bill is permitted per budget resolution. A Congress that wants to use reconciliation twice in a year must pass two separate budget resolutions." CRS R48444: "No more than one reconciliation bill may include provisions in response to each type of instruction in one budget resolution, for a maximum of three reconciliation bills." The section heading changed with it.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep): "the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97)" presented as the law's name. CRS R48444 records that the short title was struck by a Byrd-rule point of order and that the official title as enacted is "An Act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to titles II and V of the concurrent resolution on the budget for fiscal year 2018." The same is true of P.L. 117-169 and P.L. 119-21. The page now leads with that fact rather than repeating the informal names as titles - which is also the sharpest illustration of what the Byrd rule does.

REMOVED, staleness (flagged by the House-procedure batch): the list of laws enacted through reconciliation omitted P.L. 119-21, enacted 2025-07-04, and offered "multiple deficit-reduction bills in the 1990s" with no law numbers. Replaced with the CRS count (29 considered, 24 enacted since 1980; four vetoed, one failed in the Senate) and the named laws whose titles the sources actually give, including P.L. 119-21 from the stored Congress.gov public-law list.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED and wrong on the record: "In 2021, the Senate Parliamentarian ruled that a federal minimum wage increase violated the Byrd Rule, removing it from a reconciliation bill despite majority Senate support. The ruling forced the majority to find other vehicles - which they ultimately couldn't." CRS RL30862's table records a floor point of order against Sanders Amendment No. 972 during the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021: the motion to waive was rejected 42-58 on March 5, 2021, the point of order was sustained and the amendment fell. 42 is not majority support, the provision was an amendment rather than text being removed from the bill, and no source supports the "forced the majority to find other vehicles" narrative.

SOURCED, not removed (sweep F-UNSOURCED): "unless 60 senators vote to waive the rule" was correct but rested on nothing - the current text of 2 U.S.C. 644 carries no threshold, the three-fifths language having been struck from the section in 1990. CRS R48444 and RL30862 both state the threshold as three-fifths of Senators duly chosen and sworn, 60 with no more than one vacancy. Now quoted with that qualifier, matching the formulation the senate-procedure batch settled on across the audited pages.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "the most commonly invoked being:" and "This is the key test." Unsourced frequency and significance claims, and the surrounding text merged two textually distinct Byrd tests - no change in outlays or revenues, and merely incidental to non-budgetary components - into one. All six tests are now listed separately in the CRS wording.

REMOVED, U-FLAG: the invented illustrations ("A policy change that happens to save $10 million but whose primary effect is regulatory"; "A policy change that saves $10 billion") and the framing sentences "It's not a loophole or a trick", "reconciliation is the primary vehicle for major fiscal legislation when one party doesn't control 60 Senate seats" and "In each case, the majority chose reconciliation specifically because 60 Senate votes weren't available." No source states any of it. Replaced with the CRS list of what reconciliation has actually been used for.
